elements.char: Introduction
elements.label: text

elements.char: There are two complementary – and in some sense even competing – trends in modern
elements.label: text

elements.char: quantitative trading. On the one hand, more and more market participants (e.g., quantitative
elements.label: text

elements.char: traders, inter alia) employ sophisticated quantitative techniques to mine alphas.
elements.label: text

elements.char: This results in
elements.label: text

elements.char: ever fainter and more ephemeral alphas. On the other hand, technological advances allow to
elements.label: text

elements.char: essentially automate (much of) the alpha harvesting process. This yields an ever increasing
elements.label: text

elements.char: number of alphas, whose count can be in hundreds of thousands and even millions, and with
elements.label: text

elements.char: the exponentially increasing progress in this field will likely be in billions before we know it…
elements.label: text

elements.char: This proliferation of alphas – albeit mostly faint and ephemeral – allows combining them in
elements.label: text

elements.char: a sophisticated fashion to arrive at a unified “mega-alpha”. It is then this “mega-alpha” that is
elements.label: text

elements.char: actually traded – as opposed to trading individual alphas – with a bonus of automatic internal
elements.label: text

elements.char: crossing of trades (and thereby crucial-for-profitability savings on trading costs, etc.), alpha
elements.label: text

elements.char: portfolio diversification (which hedges against any subset of alphas going bust in any given time
elements.label: text

elements.char: period), and so on. One of the challenges in combining alphas is the usual “too many variables,
elements.label: text

elements.char: too few observations” dilemma. Thus, the alpha sample covariance matrix is badly singular.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Also, naturally, quantitative trading is a secretive field and data and other information from
elements.label: text

elements.char: practitioners is not readily available. This inadvertently creates an enigma around modern
elements.label: text

elements.char: quant trading. E.g., with such a large number of alphas, are they not highly correlated with
elements.label: text

elements.char: each other? What do these alphas look like? Are they mostly based on price and volume data,
elements.label: text

elements.char: mean-reversion, momentum, etc.? How do alpha returns depend on volatility, turnover, etc.?
elements.label: text

elements.char: In a previous paper [Kakushadze and Tulchinsky, 2015] took a step in demystifying the
elements.label: text

elements.char: realm of modern quantitative trading by studying some empirical properties of 4,000 real-life
elements.label: text

elements.char: alphas. In this paper we take another step and present explicit formulas – that are also
elements.label: text

elements.char: computer code – for 101 real-life quant trading alphas. Our formulaic alphas – albeit most are
elements.label: text

elements.char: not necessarily all that “simple” – serve a purpose of giving the reader a glimpse into what
elements.label: text

elements.char: some of the simpler real-life alphas look like.
elements.label: text

elements.char: It also enables the reader to replicate and test
elements.label: text

elements.char: these alphas on historical data and do new research and other empirical analyses. Hopefully, it
elements.label: text

elements.char: further inspires (young) researchers to come up with new ideas and create their own alphas.
elements.label: text

elements.char: “An alpha is a combination of mathematical expressions, computer source code, and configuration parameters
elements.label: text

elements.char: that can be used, in combination with historical data, to make predictions about future movements of various
elements.label: text

elements.char: financial instruments.” [Tulchinsky
elements.label: text

elements.char: et al
elements.label: text

elements.char: , 2015] Here “alpha” – following the common trader lingo – generally
elements.label: text

elements.char: means any reasonable “expected return” that one may wish to trade on and is not necessarily the same as the
elements.label: text

elements.char: “academic” alpha. In practice, often the detailed information about how alphas are constructed may even not be
elements.label: text

elements.char: available, e.g., the only data available could be the position data, so “alpha” then is a set of instructions to achieve
elements.label: text
